questions.question: What are ActiveRecord associations and how do you declare them?
questions.title: ActiveRecord Associations Basics
questions.direct_answer: Associations declare the links between models (a Comment belongs to a Post, a Post has many Comments) so Rails can fetch related records for you. You declare them with macros in the model: belongs_to, has_many, has_one, has_and_belongs_to_many. They rely on foreign keys in the database (post_id on comments) and give you methods like post.comments and comment.post. They're how you express 'this model is connected to that model' in code instead of writing the SQL joins yourself.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the common macros (belongs_to/has_many/has_one), what foreign key they rely on, and the convenience methods they give you.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting the foreign key convention (post_id) or confusing which side has belongs_to vs has_many.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: belongs_to/has_many/has_one declare model links; they rely on foreign keys and give you post.comments and comment.post for free.

sections.title: Macros That Wire Models Together
sections.content: ActiveRecord associations declare the links between models — a Comment belongs to a Post, a Post has many Comments — so Rails can fetch related records for you instead of you writing SQL joins. You declare them with macros in the model class: belongs_to, has_many, has_one, and has_and_belongs_to_many. They rely on foreign keys in the database (a post_id column on comments) and give you convenience methods: post.comments returns the related comments, comment.post returns the parent post. Associations are how you express 'this model is connected to that model' in code, with Rails handling the SQL.

sections.title: From Foreign Key to Method
sections.content:
A foreign key (post_id) links the tables; the association macros turn that key into a method.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Post] -->|has_many| C[Comment]
  C -->|belongs_to: post| P
  C -- post_id FK --> P.id
```

sections.title: Declaring and using associations
sections.content:
```ruby
class Comment < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :post          # comment.post -> the parent post
end

class Post < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :comments         # post.comments -> array of comments
  has_one :author            # post.author -> a single user
end

# Usage:
post = Post.first
post.comments               # all comments for this post (no SQL written by you)
comment = post.comments.create(body: 'Hi')   # sets post_id automatically
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting the foreign key convention (post_id) — the association won't find the parent.
Putting has_many on the child and belongs_to on the parent — they go the other way.
Not setting the FK when creating a child (use post.comments.create, which sets it).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Associations declare model links (belongs_to/has_many/has_one) with macros in the model.
They rely on foreign keys (post_id) and give you methods like post.comments and comment.post.
belongs_to goes on the child (the one with the FK); has_many goes on the parent.
Use post.comments.create to build a child with the FK set automatically.
They replace hand-written SQL joins for the common cases.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: ActiveRecord associations declare the links between models. A Comment belongs to a Post, and a Post has many Comments. You declare them with macros in the model: belongs_to, has_many, has_one, and has_and_belongs_to_many. They rely on foreign keys in the database, like a post_id column on comments, and give you convenience methods: post.comments returns the related comments, and comment.post returns the parent post. belongs_to goes on the child, the one with the foreign key, and has_many goes on the parent. A common mistake is forgetting the foreign key convention, because the association won't find the parent, or putting has_many on the child instead of belongs_to. Associations let you express model connections in code instead of writing SQL joins.

followup_questions: What are the common association macros (belongs_to, has_many, has_one)?
What foreign key does belongs_to rely on, and which model holds it?
What convenience methods do you get (post.comments, comment.post)?
Which side gets belongs_to vs has_many (child vs parent)?
